title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction: Context: E449 (Novi Commentarii 18, 1774) reworks Euler's theory of power residues using a primitive root a modulo a prime P. Earlier pages showed that the residues of the squares 1, 4, 9, ... coincide with the terms of the geometric progression 1, a^2, a^4, .... Scholion 56, finished on this page, generalises this. The residues of x^λ (mod P) are exactly the classes 1, a^λ, a^{2λ}, .... In modern terms, (Z/P)^* is cyclic of order P−1, and the image of the map x ↦ x^λ is the subgroup generated by a^λ, which equals the subgroup generated by a^d with d = gcd(λ, P−1). If gcd(λ, P−1) = 1 the map is a bijection and every class is a λ-th power residue. Otherwise the image has exactly (P−1)/d elements, which Euler says is evident from what precedes. He then turns to special properties of quadratic residues. Theorem 57: for P = 2n+1, −1 (i.e. 2n) is a quadratic residue iff n is even, i.e. iff P ≡ 1 (mod 4). Proof: a^n ≡ −1, since a^{2n} ≡ 1 and a^n ≢ 1 by primitivity (shown earlier in the paper). The squares are exactly the even powers of a. So if n is even, −1 = a^n appears among them. If n is odd, −1 is not an even power, because exponents are determined mod 2n and 2n is even, so it is a non-residue. This prepares Corollaries 58–59 (−1 times a residue) and Theorem 60, the Fermat two-squares step: every p ≡ 1 mod 4 divides some b^2 + x^2 with b arbitrary.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The odd-n case tacitly uses that a^k depends only on k mod 2n, so an odd exponent can never be congruent to an even one mod 2n. Euler leaves this implicit.

The whole argument rests on the existence of a primitive root. Euler's earlier proof of that in this paper was later judged incomplete (Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, art. 56). That gap concerns earlier pages, not this one.

ideas.what: λ-th power residues mod prime P form the set {a^{kλ}}; complete iff gcd(λ, P−1) = 1, otherwise exactly (P−1)/d of them, d = gcd(λ, P−1)
ideas.modern_name: Image of the λ-power map on a cyclic group; index of the subgroup of λ-th powers in (Z/p)^*
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E262, c. 1758–60, without primitive roots); systematically Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801)
ideas.where_published: E262 'Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta' (Novi Comm. 7); E449 itself

ideas.what: −1 is a quadratic residue mod p iff p ≡ 1 mod 4, proved via a^{(p−1)/2} ≡ −1 for a primitive root a
ideas.modern_name: First supplementary law of quadratic reciprocity
ideas.usually_credited_to: Fermat (statement), Euler (proofs, 1740s–1750s); primitive-root proof as in Gauss
ideas.where_published: Euler E241/E242 era papers on sums of two squares; E262; E449

deep.surprise_reason: Standard, well-documented material. The page restates Euler's own earlier results (E262) in the primitive-root framework. The primitive-root treatment in E449 is known and discussed in the histories (Weil; Gauss's commentary).
transcription_corrections: The transcription is essentially accurate; page number 112 and header confirmed. 'Theorema' is followed by article number 57; '2n' and '−1' readings are correct.
